issues: Summary says 'from January 2013 continued development was hosted as the open project Open Whisper Systems', which implies the project began then. The 21 Jan 2013 post 'A New Home' says the community had already been calling the continued work 'Open Whisper Systems' ('we've been calling the project for this continued work "Open Whisper Systems." Welcome to the project's new home'). January 2013 is when the project got its own website, not when it started under that name.

fieldFixes.summary: Whisper Systems, a mobile-security company, was acquired by Twitter in late 2011; Twitter released some of its software under the GPLv3 open-source licence, and the community's continued open development, already known as Open Whisper Systems, got its own home in January 2013. The project released Signal, free encrypted calling for iPhone, on 29 July 2014, and on 2 November 2015 began rolling out Signal for Android, combining its Android apps TextSecure (private messaging) and RedPhone (private calling) in one app.

issues: Summary says Let's Encrypt 'opened a beta in September 2015'. The beta that began in September 2015 was an invitation-only Limited Beta (started 12 September 2015). Let's Encrypt only opened to anyone with its Public Beta on 3 December 2015 (Let's Encrypt, 'Public Beta: December 3, 2015' and 'Entering Public Beta'). 'Opened' overstates the September start.

The title 'leaves beta, making HTTPS certificates free and automatic' implies that leaving beta made certificates free. Free, automated certificates had been available to everyone since the public beta of 3 December 2015; on 12 April 2016 Let's Encrypt only dropped the beta label ('The beta label is simply not necessary any more').

fieldFixes.title: Let's Encrypt leaves beta with free, automated HTTPS certificates
fieldFixes.summary: Let's Encrypt, a free, automated certificate authority run by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group — founded in May 2013 with Mozilla, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the University of Michigan, Cisco and Akamai as founding sponsors and partners — was announced on 18 November 2014, started an invitation-only Limited Beta on 12 September 2015 and opened a Public Beta to anyone on 3 December 2015. On 12 April 2016 it left beta, reporting that since the beta began it had issued more than 1.7 million certificates for more than 3.8 million websites, and stating its aim to 'encrypt 100% of the Web'.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched; --check FOUND. 'Let's Encrypt is leaving beta today.' and 'We set out to encrypt 100% of the Web.' also FOUND. The 1.7 million / 3.8 million figures are cumulative since September 2015, as the fixed summary now says.

issues: The creator field credits the crop to Duncan.Hull, which is wrong. According to the Commons file history and the API 'user' field, the cropped file was uploaded by Jochen Burghardt on 29 February 2020 ('File:Whitfield Diffie Royal Society.jpg cropped 29 % horizontally, 52 % vertically using CropTool'). Duncan.Hull uploaded the uncropped original (File:Whitfield_Diffie_Royal_Society.jpg) on 21 December 2017. He is listed on Commons as 'Author' with 'Own work', but the image is a Royal Society portrait released under VRT ticket #2014062710019796.

The licence is attributed imprecisely. 'CC BY-SA 4.0 (crop)' is not a licence on the crop specifically: the CC BY-SA 4.0 self-publication tag comes from Duncan.Hull's original upload and was copied to the crop page. The rights holder's grant is CC BY-SA 3.0 with 'Attribution: The Royal Society' (VRT-confirmed). Both are acceptable free licences, so the image stays usable. The credit line should name the Royal Society under CC BY-SA 3.0 rather than present Duncan.Hull as co-author.
